title: Phenomena-Based Inquiry Launch
preview: Students observe a real-world phenomenon and generate questions, creating an authentic need-to-know that drives the investigation for the unit.

body.summary: A phenomena-based launch presents students with a puzzling, observable real-world event and structures their initial observations, questions, and hypotheses. The phenomenon becomes the anchor for the entire unit — every lesson connects back to figuring out why this thing happens. This isn't a hook that you forget after day 1. It's the driving question that makes students NEED to learn the science.
body.whenToUse:
Use at the beginning of a new unit or topic. The phenomenon should be:
• Observable — students can see/hear/experience it (video, demo, image, data)
• Puzzling — it should make students go "Wait, what? Why does that happen?"
• Complex — it can't be fully explained in one lesson
• Connected — the science content you're teaching actually explains it

Examples: Why does a heavy cargo ship float but a small coin sinks? Why are there different rock types on the same mountain? Why do some materials get hot in the sun and others don't?
body.howToImplement:
1. PRESENT THE PHENOMENON (2-3 min): Show a video, image, demonstration, or data set. Say nothing — just let students observe. Don't explain. Don't preview. Let the phenomenon speak for itself.

2. NOTICE (2 min): Say: "Write down everything you NOTICE. Just observations — no explanations yet." Students write silently on sticky notes or in their notebooks.

3. WONDER (2 min): Say: "Now write down everything you WONDER. What questions do you have?" Students write silently.

4. SHARE (3-4 min): Students share with a partner, then contribute to a class list. Record ALL questions on a large chart paper or whiteboard. Don't evaluate or answer any questions.

5. CATEGORIZE (2-3 min): As a class, sort questions:
   • Questions we can investigate (testable)
   • Questions we need to research (look up)
   • Questions we can't answer yet (need more info)

6. DRIVING QUESTION (2 min): Together, select or craft a driving question for the unit. Post it prominently. Say: "Everything we do in this unit will help us figure out the answer to this question."

7. REVISIT THROUGHOUT: Come back to the phenomenon board regularly: "Based on what we learned today, can we answer any of our questions? Do we have new ones?"
body.teacherMoves:
IF students jump straight to explanations instead of observations:
→ Redirect: "That's a great EXPLANATION, but right now I only want OBSERVATIONS. What do you SEE? Save the why for later."
→ Model: "I notice the water changes color" (observation) vs. "The water changes color because of a chemical reaction" (explanation). We want the first one right now."

IF students can't generate questions:
→ Prompt with starters: "Why does ___? What would happen if ___? How is ___ possible?"
→ Show the phenomenon again and ask: "What surprised you? What didn't you expect?"
→ Give a ridiculous question yourself to lower the bar: "I wonder if aliens caused this. No? Okay, what DO you think caused it?" Humor helps.

IF students generate only surface-level questions:
→ Push deeper: "That's a good question. Now ask a follow-up: WHY does that happen? What's causing it?"
→ Model: "Your question is 'Does it always do that?' A deeper version might be 'What conditions cause it to do that?'"

IF students lose interest after day 1:
→ The phenomenon board is your tool. Start each lesson by pointing to it: "Remember our phenomenon? Today we're going to figure out [specific piece]."
→ Add new evidence to the board as the unit progresses — new data, new observations.
→ Have students update their initial explanations: "Look at what you wrote on day 1. How has your thinking changed?"

IF the phenomenon doesn't puzzle students (they think they already know):
→ Add a twist: "Okay, you said it's because of ___. Then explain THIS..." (show a case that contradicts their simple explanation).
→ Say: "You might be right. Let's see if the data supports that. What evidence would we need?"
body.variations:
TIER 1 (Core):
Use as described above. Build a physical or digital "phenomenon board" that stays up all unit. Students add to it as they learn more.

TIER 2 (Scaffolded):
Provide observation and questioning frames:
• "I notice ___ (what I see/hear/observe)."
• "I wonder ___ (my question about what I observed)."
• "I think ___ might be happening because ___."
• "One thing that surprises me is ___."

Show the phenomenon twice — once to just watch, and once with specific prompts: "This time, watch what happens to the [specific thing]. Write down what you see."

For ELL students: Provide a labeled diagram or vocabulary list related to the phenomenon.

TIER 2 (Alternative — Guided Phenomenon):
Instead of open-ended Notice/Wonder, provide 3 specific observation questions:
1. "What do you see happening to [A]?"
2. "What changes about [B]?"
3. "How does [A] compare to [B]?"
Then ask: "Based on your observations, what question could we investigate?"

ADVANCED EXTENSION:
Students find their own phenomenon related to the topic (from news, YouTube, or personal experience) and present it to the class with a driving question. The class votes on which phenomenon to investigate further.
body.researchBase: NGSS emphasizes anchoring instruction in phenomena to make science relevant and to develop students' abilities to figure out how the world works (NRC, 2012). Krajcik and Shin (2022) demonstrate that phenomena-based instruction increases engagement and conceptual understanding, particularly for students from non-dominant backgrounds. Windschitl and Thompson (2006) found that anchoring phenomena provide a coherent storyline that helps students connect individual lessons to big ideas.
